sourceText: The DELANY-BABEL17 sector was already in progress when they entered. For several lessons Aster had refused to pause worlds for their arrival; the fact that a class was visiting was not a cosmic event for the inhabitants. Marae learns a language that makes certain strategies feel so natural that her preferences begin to change. The memorial bore the name of Samuel R. Delany — Babel-17 precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Information was not merely something that circulated between agents. Sometimes it changed the agent, sometimes the environment, and in the most dangerous cases it changed the criterion by which truth could be recognized. Marae kept her local body vulnerable. Pain, fatigue, and the impossibility of doing ten things at once were epistemic instruments for her, not biological scenery. 201 The children were met by Mina, who refused demonstrations. ‘If you can perform miracles, perform them after you tell me what becomes irreversible.’ Marae appreciated the formulation; Aster admitted that in earlier eras she herself would have asked the question only after optimizing. The problem closed quickly around them: Her siblings cannot decide whether she has been manipulated or has gained access to a genuine perspective they do not possess. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Lu — Cognitive Language: language changes the space of thought; Ci — Self-Interpreting Code: executable text modifies its interpreter. Course references included Samuel R. Delany — Babel-17; metacomputational fiction. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Vela broke the first consensus. ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ Tern answered without raising their voice: ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. 202 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS The White Hunger appeared in Aster as a loss of relief. She did not lack entertainment. She lacked the resistance of things to the model. When she could anticipate every reaction, the world became functionally an extension of her own mind, and the presence of the other thinned toward simulacrum. Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules. The night did not end in victory. Aster classifies language as a technology that changes the space of decisions, not merely as a channel. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern no longer called the anomaly a “signal.” He used the more modest term residue. He found it only after excluding the explanations he wanted to be true. Vela helped precisely through skepticism: if a hypothesis survived a sister motivated to destroy it, it deserved another night. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the EXTERNALIZATION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — turns an internal property into an object, companion, 203 infrastructure, or institution — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. When the threshold closed, Aster remained silent one second longer than protocol required. The children had already noticed that this was her smallest unit of fear. 204 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
